hints: Think about what volatility really means, how easily a liquid turns to vapour by breaking forces between molecules.
Compare $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Br}_2$, bromine has many more electrons so its electron cloud is larger and more easily distorted.
Link stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces to needing more energy to separate molecules, and so to lower volatility.
walkthrough:
**Recall what volatility means**

Think of volatility as how easily molecules escape from liquid to gas. More volatile means weaker intermolecular forces to break.

Rule: stronger forces = less volatile, weaker forces = more volatile.

**Identify the forces in halogens**

Both chlorine ($\text{Cl}_2$) and bromine ($\text{Br}_2$) are simple non-polar molecules. The only forces between them are instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, also called London forces.

**Compare strength in chlorine vs bromine**

Bromine has more electrons (35 per atom vs 17 for chlorine) and a larger electron cloud. This makes it more polarisable, so temporary dipoles form more easily.

$$ \text{strength of London forces: } \text{Br}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 $$

**Deduce volatility**

Because forces are stronger in bromine, more energy is needed to separate $\text{Br}_2$ molecules. So bromine is less volatile and chlorine is more volatile. This is why chlorine is a gas and bromine is a liquid at room temperature.

options.A: Incorrect. The explanation part is right that forces are greater in bromine, but the conclusion is backwards. Stronger forces mean harder to vaporise, so bromine is the less volatile element, not the more volatile.
options.B: Incorrect on both parts. Bromine is not more volatile, and forces are not greater in chlorine. Students choosing this may have reversed the trend that larger molecules with more electrons have stronger London forces.
options.C: Correct. Chlorine is more volatile because its instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces are weaker. Bromine has more electrons and is more polarisable, so its London forces are stronger and it is less easy to vaporise.
options.D: Incorrect. Chlorine is indeed the more volatile element, but the reason given is wrong. Forces are weaker in chlorine, not greater. Stronger forces belong to bromine due to its larger electron cloud.
